claims.text: Controlled selective dealloying of an NM-HEA precursor containing less-noble sacrificial elements will produce a three-dimensional nanoporous nanoframework.
The resulting nanoframework will preserve a high-entropy atomic distribution.
The resulting nanoframework will enhance catalytic activity.
The precursor contains noble and sacrificial elements in near-equiatomic ratios.
The precursor forms a homogeneous solid solution.
Chemical or electrochemical dealloying can selectively dissolve the sacrificial elements.
An electrolyte potential or chemical environment can be selected to favor removal of less-noble elements from the NM-HEA.
Liquid-cell TEM can monitor the nanoscale evolution of the NM-HEA during dealloying.
Selective dealloying forms interconnected porous channels and ligaments within the HEA.
The interconnected channels and ligaments constitute a three-dimensional nanoframework.
Selective dissolution creates vacancy pathways and initial nanopores.
The remaining noble elements rearrange while maintaining a high-entropy distribution.
Real-time TEM feedback can be used to adjust dealloying parameters and achieve atomic-scale precision.
The nanoporous framework will have significantly greater surface area than the undealloyed precursor.
Maintained compositional uniformity and increased surface area will improve catalytic efficiency relative to the undealloyed precursor.
The pristine NM-HEA precursor lacks the desired three-dimensional nanoporous structure.
Incomplete removal of sacrificial elements or poorly controlled dealloying rates can limit framework formation or disrupt the high-entropy distribution.
Extreme dealloying conditions may cause structural collapse or phase segregation.

High-entropy nanoalloys can be efficient and stable catalysts because elemental interactions, lattice distortions, and crystalline defects can enhance reactivity and create preferential reaction sites.
